subject: phy
title: Work, Energy and Power
subtitle: Work done, kinetic and potential energy, efficiency and power.
concept: Work is done when a force causes displacement in the direction of the force: W = Fs cosθ.
The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
Energy is conserved in all processes; power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy.

notes.heading: Work Done
items: Work is done when a force has a component in the direction of displacement: W = Fs cosθ, where θ is the angle between the force and the direction of motion. If θ = 90°, no work is done (e.g. centripetal force, normal reaction on horizontal motion). The SI unit is the joule (J = N m).
The area under a force–displacement graph equals the work done, even for non-constant forces.

notes.heading: Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem
items: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔEₖ = ½mv² − ½mu².
Kinetic energy: Eₖ = ½mv². Gravitational potential energy: Eₚ = mgh (relative to a chosen reference level). Elastic potential energy (Hooke's law spring): E_el = ½kx².

Conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted between forms. In a closed system, total mechanical energy (Eₖ + Eₚ) is constant when only conservative forces act. In practice, non-conservative forces (friction, air resistance) convert mechanical energy to thermal energy.

notes.heading: Power and Efficiency
items: Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy: P = W/t = ΔE/Δt (watts, W = J s⁻¹). For a constant driving force: P = Fv. At terminal velocity, the driving force equals the resistive force and P = Fv gives the power output needed to maintain constant speed.

Efficiency = useful output power / total input power (or useful output energy / total input energy). Expressed as a decimal (0–1) or percentage (0–100%). Always < 1 in practice — some energy is always dissipated as heat.

definitions.body: W = Fs cosθ; work is done when a force has a component in the direction of displacement; units: joule (J).
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔEk.
The rate of doing work or transferring energy: P = W/t = ΔE/Δt; SI unit: watt (W).
The ratio of useful output energy (or power) to total input energy (or power); always ≤ 1 (or ≤ 100%).

workedExamples.q: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates from 10 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹. Calculate the work done by the engine (assume no friction).
A pump lifts 50 kg of water 8 m every minute. Calculate its minimum power output. (g = 10 m s⁻²)

mistakes: Forgetting the cosθ factor in W = Fs cosθ when force and displacement are not parallel.
Confusing power (W = J s⁻¹) with energy (J).
Using P = Fv for the wrong quantity — at terminal velocity, F = resistive force, not net force.
tips: W = Fs cosθ: if the angle is 90°, cos90° = 0, so no work is done (e.g. centripetal force, normal reaction).
At terminal velocity: acceleration = 0, so driving force = total resistive force; P = Fv gives engine power.
Efficiency < 100% always — energy is always lost to surroundings, usually as thermal energy.

flashcards.q: State the formula for work done by a force at an angle.
flashcards.a: W = Fs cosθ (F = force, s = displacement, θ = angle between force and displacement).
Net work done on a body = change in its kinetic energy: W_net = ΔEk = ½mv² − ½mu².

flashcards.q: What is the formula for power in terms of force and velocity?
flashcards.a: P = Fv (watts, when F in N and v in m s⁻¹).
Efficiency = useful output power / input power (or useful output energy / input energy); expressed as fraction or %.

flashcards.q: A spring with k = 200 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 0.05 m. What is the elastic PE stored?
Why does a centripetal force do no work?
flashcards.a: The centripetal force is always perpendicular to the velocity (and displacement), so θ = 90° and cos90° = 0 → W = 0.

questions.q: A 5 N force moves an object 4 m at 60° to the force. How much work is done?
A 2 kg ball falls from rest through 5 m (g = 10 m s⁻²). What is its speed at the bottom?
questions.exp: Energy conservation: ½mv² = mgh; v² = 2gh = 2×10×5 = 100; v = 10 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A motor has input power 500 W and lifts a mass at 200 W useful output. What is its efficiency?
A car travels at constant 20 m s⁻¹ against a resistive force of 600 N. What engine power is needed?
questions.exp: P = Fv = 600×20 = 12 000 W = 12 kW. At terminal velocity, driving force equals resistive force.

questions.q: What does the area under a force–displacement graph represent?
questions.exp: Area under F–s graph = ∫F ds = work done.

recall: Calculate work done using W = Fs cosθ.
Apply the work-energy theorem to find speed changes.
Calculate power from work done or from P = Fv.
Calculate efficiency given input and output power.
Explain why no work is done by a centripetal force.
